issues.legal_issue: Special deductions for mineral-oil operations are unavailable when the governing agreement does not specify them.
material_facts: The taxpayer claimed special deductions for drilling and exploration expenditure and depletion of mineral oil.
The signed production-sharing contracts contained no provision granting the claimed deductions.
The tax authority disallowed the deductions because the contracts did not include the required stipulation.
issues.conclusion: The taxpayer was not entitled to the deductions because the signed contracts did not provide for them.
issues.legal_principle: Section 42 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 permits specified special allowances only in relation to a qualifying agreement with the Central Government, laid before each House of Parliament, that specifies the allowances and the manner of computing them. The agreement governs this special accounting regime; without the required stipulations, the Assessing Officer cannot allow the deductions. The Court relied on Commissioner of Income Tax, Dehradun v. Enron Oil and Gas India Ltd. (2008) 15 SCC 33, and distinguished the estoppel point in CIT v. Enron Expat Service Inc. (2010) 327 ITR 626.

predicates.tax_deduction_claim_in_assessment: A taxpayer claimed a special deduction while its income was being assessed.
predicates.qualifying_mineral_oil_business: The taxpayer carried on a business involving the prospecting for, extraction of, or production of mineral oil.
predicates.signed_agreement_lacks_claimed_allowance: The agreement governing the business did not specify the special allowance claimed.

issues.definition: When a taxpayer claims a special deduction in an assessment for a qualifying mineral-oil business, omission of that allowance from the governing agreement means the taxpayer is not entitled to it.

issues.legal_issue: Terms of a model contract cannot be incorporated into a signed contract that makes itself the complete and exclusive agreement.
material_facts: A model production-sharing contract contained a provision for the claimed tax deductions.

The signed production-sharing contracts defined the contract by reference to their own terms and appendices, superseded earlier understandings, and required written agreement by all parties for amendment.
The signed contracts did not incorporate the model contract's deduction provision.
issues.conclusion: The model contract could not be read into the signed contracts, and the tax authority had to assess the claim by reference to the signed contracts alone.
issues.legal_principle: The terms of an executed contract control where the parties have made it the complete agreement and have expressly superseded earlier agreements or understandings. The Court applied the contract's entire-agreement and amendment clauses and treated the signed production-sharing contracts as the exclusive repository of their terms.

predicates.contract_interpretation_proceeding: A dispute requires a court or decision-maker to determine the terms of an executed contract.
predicates.signed_contract_is_complete_agreement: The executed contract states that it supersedes prior agreements or understandings and is the complete agreement between the parties.
predicates.model_terms_not_expressly_incorporated: The executed contract does not expressly incorporate the relevant terms of a model or earlier agreement.

issues.definition: In a contract interpretation dispute, model terms are not part of an executed contract when that contract is complete and does not incorporate those terms.

issues.legal_issue: An erroneous allowance of deductions in earlier years does not create an entitlement to continue receiving them.
material_facts: Tax authorities had allowed the deductions in earlier assessment years under the same contracts.
The contracts did not provide for those deductions, so the earlier allowances were legally erroneous.
The taxpayer relied on those earlier allowances in claiming the deductions for a later assessment year.
issues.conclusion: The earlier allowances did not entitle the taxpayer to deductions in the later assessment year; there is no estoppel against the law.
issues.legal_principle: A prior error by a tax authority cannot require the same error to be repeated, and there is no estoppel against law. The Court applied the principle in CIT v. Enron Expat Service Inc. (2010) 327 ITR 626, which held that an earlier tax treatment did not estop a taxpayer from claiming the treatment legally available for a later year, and applied the same principle to an earlier benefit wrongly granted by the authorities.

predicates.income_tax_assessment_case: A dispute concerns the deductions available in an income-tax assessment.
predicates.prior_deduction_allowed: The tax authority allowed the same deduction in an earlier assessment period.
predicates.governing_contract_does_not_authorize_de: The agreement governing the taxpayer's business does not provide for the deduction.

issues.definition: In an income-tax assessment, an earlier allowance does not create an entitlement to a deduction that the governing agreement does not authorize.

issues.legal_issue: A court ordinarily will not use writ jurisdiction to compel amendment of a purely contractual agreement where no public-law element or right to amendment is established.
material_facts: The taxpayer sought writ relief requiring the Government to add a tax-deduction term to executed production-sharing contracts.
The contracts required amendments to be made in writing and signed by all parties, and the Government had not agreed to the requested amendment.
The contracts were formal government contracts, but the dispute concerned contractual rights and did not involve a public-law element warranting writ relief.
The taxpayer had an alternative tax appeal pending.
issues.conclusion: The taxpayer had no right to compel amendment of the contracts, and this was not a fit case for writ relief; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Writ relief is not absolutely barred in contractual disputes involving the State, but it is ordinarily unavailable for a purely contractual claim without a public-law element; the High Court retains discretion and may decline relief where an alternative contractual or statutory remedy exists. A contract requiring a written amendment signed by all parties gives no unilateral right to amendment. Formal government contracts must also satisfy Article 299 of the Constitution, and their novation must meet the applicable procedural requirements. The Court relied on Andi Mukta Sadguru v. R. Rudani (1989) 2 SCC 691; Bareilly Development Authority v. Ajai Pal Singh (1989) 1 SCR 743; Divisional Forest Officer v. Bishwanath Tea Co. Ltd. (1981) 3 SCR 662; Kumari Shrilekha Vidyarthi v. State of U.P. (1991) 1 SCC 212; State of Gujarat v. M.P. Shah Charitable Trust (1994) 3 SCC 552; ABL International Ltd. v. Export Credit Guarantee Corporation (2004) 3 SCC 553; and LIC of India v. Escorts Ltd. (1986) 1 SCC 264.

rule.if: writ_proceeding_over_state_contract and dispute_is_purely_contractual and no_public_law_element and relief_requires_compelled_amendment and no_mutual_written_amendment_agreement

predicates.writ_proceeding_over_state_contract: A claimant seeks writ relief concerning a contract to which the State or its instrumentality is a party.
predicates.dispute_is_purely_contractual: The claim concerns rights and obligations arising only from the contract.
predicates.no_public_law_element: The challenged conduct does not involve a public-law duty or a demonstrated public-law defect such as arbitrary State action.
predicates.relief_requires_compelled_amendment: The requested relief would require the State to change the terms of an executed contract.
predicates.no_mutual_written_amendment_agreement: The parties have not agreed in a signed writing to the proposed contract amendment.

issues.definition: A writ court should not compel amendment of a State contract when the dispute is purely contractual, no public-law element is shown, and the parties have not agreed in writing to the amendment.
